children.text: Pool projects rarely go wrong during construction. They go wrong in the two weeks before it, when decisions get deferred because nobody realizes they are about to become permanent.

Once the excavator is on site, the shape of the hole, where the equipment lives and how water leaves your yard are all settled. This is the list worth working through first, ordered roughly by how expensive each one is to change afterwards.
The three that are genuinely hard to undo
If you read nothing else, settle these:
It drives setbacks, the equipment run, drainage and the enclosure footprint.
A spa shares structure with the pool. Adding one later means cutting into a finished shell.
Whether a screen enclosure is coming.
The deck has to be built to carry it, whether or not it goes up on day one.
Everything else on this list is easier to revisit. These three are not.
Setbacks decide what is legal. Sun, sightlines and the house decide what is pleasant.

A pool pushed to the rear setback maximizes deck between the house and the water, which is usually where people actually sit. A pool close to the house shortens the plumbing run and keeps the kids in view from the kitchen. Both are defensible; they are different houses to live in.
Worth checking before you commit: where the afternoon sun lands in summer, and what the neighbours see.

Decide now. An integrated spa shares a wall with the pool; a spillover spa sits raised and returns water over a weir. Both are structural, and both are part of the shell that gets formed and poured once.

If an enclosure is likely within a few years, building the deck to take it costs very little now and saves cutting a finished deck later. If it is definitely not coming, you can spend that deck budget on surface instead. What is expensive is not deciding — see

children.text: 4. How equipment gets to the back yard

This one surprises people. If a mini-excavator cannot physically reach your yard — a narrow side gate, a neighbour's wall, a mature tree in the only route — the work happens by hand or by crane, and the whole project carries a surcharge.

Walk the route yourself before anyone quotes. Measure the narrowest point. If it is tight, say so early: it changes the number, and a builder who discovers it on day one has to change the number anyway.
Rock, a high water table and old fill all change excavation. None of them are visible from the surface, and all of them are cheaper to find out about before the contract than during the dig.
Florida rain arrives fast and in quantity. A new pool and a new deck replace absorbent yard with hard surface, which has to drain somewhere that is not your slab or your neighbour's.
Drainage is designed alongside the deck, not added to it. If you are also planning
, plan the two together — the grading serves both.
Pumps and heaters need somewhere to live: reachable for service, close enough to keep the plumbing run short, and far enough from bedroom windows that nobody minds the noise.
The default is "wherever there is space down the side of the house". It is worth five minutes of thought, because moving it later means re-running plumbing and electrical.
8. Heating, and what it costs to run
Heating decides how many months a year the pool is usable, which for most families decides whether it gets used at all.
It also changes the plumbing and the electrical service, so it belongs before the shell, not after. The choice between a heat pump and gas is a running-cost question more than a purchase question.

A salt system and traditional chlorine end up in the same chemistry; they differ in how you handle it day to day and in what the water feels like. Salt also has implications for the materials around the pool, which is a reason to decide it alongside the deck rather than after.

children.text: Pool lights are run before the shell is finished. The number is a decision, not a detail: too few leaves dark water at the ends, and the usual mistake is one light in a pool long enough to need three.
Think about the deck and the yard at the same time — the pool is rarely the only thing you want lit after dark.

are all cheaper built while the crews, the access and the slab work are already on site.
You do not have to build them now. You do want to know where they go, so the pool and the deck leave room and the sleeves and conduit go in while the ground is open.

Work backwards. A Florida pool project runs through permitting, excavation, steel, plumbing, shell, tile and deck, finish and startup — with inspections between stages that have to pass before the next begins.

children.text: Most people choose a pool builder by collecting three quotes and picking the middle one. That compares prices, which is the one thing about a pool project that is easy to compare and the least predictive of how it goes.
These are the ten questions worth asking instead. None of them are gotchas — a good builder will have quick, specific answers, and the speed of the answer tells you nearly as much as its content.
Is the license held by the company I am contracting with, and does it cover pool construction?
Who runs my job day to day, and how do I reach them?
How are changes priced and approved once work has started?
Licensing tells you whether the work can be permitted and inspected. The second tells you what the next few months feel like. The third is where most disputes actually begin.
1. What license do you hold, and in whose name?
Pool construction in Florida is a licensed trade with its own classification. A general contractor's license is not the same thing.

Ask for the number, then check it yourself on the state's public lookup. Two things to confirm beyond "active": that the classification covers pool and spa work, and that the name on the license matches the entity on your contract. Work sold by one company and permitted under another's license is a real pattern, and it is the homeowner who is left holding it.
2. Who is actually on my job?
There is a difference between the person who sells the project and the person who runs it. Ask who that second person is, how many jobs they carry at once, and how you reach them.
A specific answer — a name, a phone number, a normal response window — is a good sign. "Someone will always get back to you" is not an answer.

blog.alt: Raised spa with a spillway returning to the pool, framed by a travertine deck beside a single-storey home.

children.text: 3. Is this quote the same scope as the others?
Two pool quotes are almost never for the same thing. One includes the equipment pad relocation, another does not. One assumes standard access, another has walked the side gate.

Put them side by side and compare line by line, not total by total. Where one is silent, ask what happens if that item turns out to be needed. A builder who says "that would be a change order" is being straight with you; the number to be suspicious of is the one with no line items at all.
The decisions that move the price are covered in
what a custom pool really costs
— worth reading before the comparison, so you know which lines to look for.

Ask directly. The honest list usually contains some of: utility relocation, unexpected rock, dewatering a high water table, HOA submissions, landscape restoration outside the work area, and the electrical service upgrade a heater sometimes needs.
None of those are red flags as exclusions. They are red flags as surprises.
The answer you want: in writing, priced, signed before the work happens.

Verbal changes that appear on the final invoice are the most common source of pool disputes, and the fix is entirely procedural. Agree at the outset that nothing changes without a signed order, and the rest of the project gets easier.
6. What does the payment schedule track?

Payments should follow completed stages, not the calendar. A schedule tied to inspected milestones means you are never far ahead of the work and the builder is never funding your job out of the next one.
Be careful with large deposits before anything is permitted, and with a schedule where the final payment is too small to matter — the last 5% is what gets the punch list finished.

The contractor should, under their own license. A builder who asks the homeowner to pull an owner-builder permit is transferring the liability for the work to you, and most people who agree to it do not realize that is what happened.
Permits also tell you about scope: pool, electrical, plumbing and any enclosure or barrier are separate reviews.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
covers what a full set looks like.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a pool and raised spa on a travertine deck, with a garden hose coiled at the edge of the lawn.

children.text: 8. What happens if an inspection fails?
Failed inspections happen. The useful question is what the process is when one does — who reschedules, how quickly, and whether the delay is absorbed or billed.
A builder who says inspections never fail is telling you either that they do not do many, or that they are managing your expectations rather than the project.
9. What is the warranty, and on what exactly?

A pool has several different warranties layered on top of each other: the shell, the interior finish, the equipment (manufacturer, not builder) and the labor. They have different lengths and different exclusions.
Ask for them separately and in writing. "Fully warrantied" as a single phrase covers nothing you can rely on later.
10. Can I talk to someone whose pool you finished two years ago?

Anyone can supply a reference from last month. The interesting call is with a customer far enough past completion to have had something go slightly wrong, because the answer you are listening for is how it was handled.
Ask that customer one question: when you called about something after the final payment, what happened?

It is tempting to treat this as a scorecard. It is more useful as a conversation. What you are really assessing is whether the answers are specific, whether they are consistent across the meeting, and whether the person answering seems to expect the question.
The builder who has thought about failed inspections, exclusions and change orders before you asked is the one who has run enough projects to have needed a process.
